title: How to Avoid Burnout in Ministry
subtitle: The hidden causes of pastoral burnout, the early warning signs every minister ignores, and the slow obedient recovery that gets a leader back to a soul that works.

sections.title: No One Burns Out Doing What They Hate
sections.body:
Burnout does not come for the lazy. It comes for the devoted. It comes for the man who loved the work so much he stopped asking whether the work was killing him.

I have been there. I told myself I was being faithful. I was answering the late call, taking the extra meeting, writing the better sermon, sitting longer at the hospital bed, and I called all of it obedience. It was not obedience. It was a slow refusal to believe that God could run the church without me running myself into the ground. The flesh hides well inside the language of service. A man can grind his soul to powder and receive applause for it the whole way down.

Burnout is not weakness. It is devotion that forgot it was a creature and started acting like a savior.

sections.title: The Body Tells the Truth the Mouth Will Not
sections.body:
The first sign is not exhaustion. The first sign is the loss of joy in the things that once carried joy. You used to love the study. Now you dread the blank page. You used to feel the weight of a person in front of you. Now you feel only the clock.

Then comes the cynicism. People become problems to be managed instead of souls to be loved. Then comes the numbness, which is the heart pulling its hand back from a stove it has touched too many times. Then the sleep goes. Then the prayer goes, because you cannot bring yourself before God when you are this angry at the life He gave you.

The body keeps a record the soul tries to deny. The chest tightens. The temper shortens. The wife notices before the elders do. Listen to her. She is reading a gauge you have learned to stop checking.

sections.title: You Are Not the Fourth Person of the Trinity
sections.body:
Underneath every burned out pastor is a quiet heresy. The heresy says the kingdom depends on me. It never says it out loud. It works in the dark, in the calendar, in the inability to say no, in the conviction that if I stop the whole thing falls.

The whole thing does not fall. Jesus built His church before you were born and He will hold it after you are gone. The work was never yours to carry alone. He invited you into a labor He was already doing and will finish whether you sleep tonight or not.

Not a hired hand who must save the flock. A shepherd under the Shepherd who already did.

sections.title: Recovery Is Slow and It Is Obedient
sections.body:
There is no quick fix for a soul run dry. The man who ran himself empty over three years does not refill in a weekend at the lake. He refills the way a field recovers after it has been worked too hard. By rest. By season. By being left alone long enough to remember what it was made for.

Start with sleep, which is the most spiritual thing an exhausted man can do. Then the small disciplines you abandoned. The walk. The Psalm read slowly with no sermon hiding inside it. The honest friend who is allowed to ask how you actually are. Then the harder work of cutting. Some things you carry must be set down and never picked up again, and you will grieve them, and that grief is part of the cure.

Recovery is not earning your way back to usefulness. It is learning again that you were loved before you were useful.

sections.title: Build the Walls Before You Need Them
sections.body:
The pastor who recovers and changes nothing will be back in the ditch by next winter. Avoiding burnout is not a one time rescue. It is a way of living built on the conviction that you are a man and not a machine.

Guard the day off as you guard your doctrine. Keep one friend who knows everything. Let the church learn to function when you are away, because a church that cannot survive your vacation is a church you have quietly taught to worship you. Pray more than you produce. Measure the week by faithfulness and not by output, because output is the drug that got you here.

The goal was never a busy man who collapsed at sixty. The goal was a faithful man still standing at eighty, still tender, still glad. That man rests on purpose. Build the walls now.
